records.sourceFile: Radiographic Analysis of National Football League Players’ Fifth Metatarsal Morphology Relationship to Proximal Fifth Metatarsal Fracture Risk.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Retrospective case-control study of 96 feet from 51 athletes, drawn from NFL players treated for zone 2 fifth metatarsal fractures between 1992 and 2012 and 2014 NFL Combine participants with foot radiographs; 15 feet had fractures and 81 did not. Two reviewers measured fifth metatarsal morphology and foot type on AP, lateral and oblique radiographs. Fractured feet had a narrower apex medullary canal on AP views, a smaller fourth-fifth intermetatarsal angle, greater fifth metatarsal angle and less talar head uncovering, and on lateral views a longer fifth metatarsal and lower apex height, fifth metatarsal angle and talocalcaneal angle.
records.limitations: Small sample with only 15 fractured feet, a convenience sample, a retrospective design and incomplete Combine records. Comparisons used multiple t tests with no correction, and the study cannot show that the morphology causes fracture.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the morphology differences as a screening tool that identifies players who will fracture, but the paper is a small retrospective comparison and does not test any screen or footwear intervention.

records.sourceFile: Recalibrating the risk of hamstring strain injury (HSI) - A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis of risk factors for index and recurrent HSI in sport.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Systematic review and meta-analysis updating a 2013 review, covering 78 prospective studies of 71,324 athletes with 8,319 hamstring strain injuries (HSIs), including 967 recurrences. The sample was mostly elite, predominantly male, and mainly football, Australian football and track and field. Older age, any previous HSI (RR 2.7), a recent HSI in the same season (RR 4.8), previous ACL injury (RR 1.7) and previous calf strain (RR 1.5) were significantly associated with HSI risk, while none of 13 strength-related variables were significantly associated in the meta-analysis.
records.limitations: Pooled estimates depend on mostly observational studies, 60% of which were rated high risk of bias, and injury definitions and the index versus recurrent classification varied across studies. Many best evidence synthesis findings rest on one or a few studies, and the search was limited to English-language full-text publications.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read these population-level associations as an individual screening tool, when the authors describe HSI as multifactorial and the associations as modest and interacting.

records.sourceFile: Recent Trends in Quadriceps Tendon and Patellar Tendon Injuries in the National Football League.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Descriptive epidemiology study of publicly available NFL injury reports and Pro Football Focus grades for the 2009-2010 to 2022-2023 seasons. It identified 80 extensor tendon tears (24 quadriceps, 56 patellar) in 77 players, and 96.3% were season ending. Return to play was 58.3% after quadriceps tendon tears and 55.4% after patellar tendon tears, and 33.3% and 21.4% of these groups, respectively, returned to prior performance within 2 seasons.
records.limitations: Injury data came from public reports, so some tears may have been missed, and detail on tear grade, side and treatment was limited. The sample is small (24 quadriceps and 56 patellar tears), there was no comparison group, and many subgroup comparisons rest on cells of 1 to 3 players.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the age, BMI, position and experience associations as predictors for an individual player, when they come from small subgroups of publicly reported NFL injuries with no control group.

records.sourceFile: Recurrent Anterior Cruciate Ligament Tears in the National Football League A Case-Control Study.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: A matched cohort study (level 3 evidence) using NFL Combine orthopaedic evaluations from 2006 to 2012 and internet-based follow-up. It compared 100 drafted players with a prior successful ACL reconstruction against 200 position- and draft-matched players without prior ACL injury. Subsequent ACL injury in the NFL occurred in 25% of the reconstructed group (26 injuries) versus 9% of controls (18 injuries; P < .001), at a mean of 22.1 months after the draft.
records.limitations: Injury outcomes were ascertained from public internet sources rather than prospective surveillance, and the study does not record injury mechanism, graft type, or playing surface. Players who were drafted without an invitation to the Combine could not be captured.
records.synthesisCaution: The 25% vs 9% difference describes NFL players who had already been drafted, so it should not be read as a general ACL re-injury rate for all athletes or as proof that prior reconstruction causes re-injury.

records.sourceFile: Recurrent and subsequent injuries in professional and elite sport - A systematic review.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: A PRISMA systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42019119264) of prospective injury surveillance studies in professional or elite football, rugby, athletics, cricket and multi-sport events, searched to July 2020. Of 81 eligible studies, 30 did not report recurrent injuries, leaving 51 for data extraction. Where recurrent injuries were reported, their proportion of all injuries ranged from 5.5% to 48%, and in the few studies using subsequent injury models most subsequent injuries (51 to 80%) were different and unrelated to the index injury.
records.limitations: The review is limited to English-language studies of professional and elite sport with a published consensus definition, so amateur and collegiate data are excluded. Many included studies pooled data across seasons and scored low on the Downs and Black quality checklist, which limits how precisely their injury rates can be compared.
records.synthesisCaution: The recurrent-injury proportions describe how injuries were recorded in pooled surveillance data, not how often an individual athlete re-injures the same tissue, so they should not be read as a measured re-injury risk.

records.sourceFile: Reduced match exposure in the previous 2 matches accounts for hamstring muscle injury incidence in professional football players.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: A prospective controlled observational study over three LaLiga seasons in two professional teams. Thirty-seven hamstring strain injuries in 23 outfield players were each paired 1:1 with an uninjured starter in the same position and team. Lower cumulative playing time, distance and high-speed running in the one and two matches before injury were associated with higher injury risk (for example, playing time relative risk 1.41 per 10 min in the match before injury), while the three- and four-match windows were not significant for playing time.
records.limitations: Training load was not recorded, and injuries occurred in both matches (86.4%) and training (13.6%). Data came from two teams over three seasons, and the cut-off points have low sensitivity (36% to 64%), so many injured players would not have been flagged.
records.synthesisCaution: Low match minutes in the previous two games were linked with hamstring injury, but this is an association in matched pairs from two teams, and the cut-offs should not be used as a screening threshold that predicts which individual player will be injured.

records.sourceFile: Regular season injury rates in the National Football League after an attenuated preseason due to COVID-19.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: A descriptive epidemiology study that used public NFL injury records to compare musculoskeletal injuries in the 2019 regular season (632 injuries) with the 2020 regular season, which followed a cancelled COVID-19 preseason (765 injuries, P=.0324, Wilcoxon signed-rank). The authors report significant increases in calf or Achilles strains (17 vs 39), groin injuries (25 vs 46) and ACL tears (14 vs 29), and a non-significant rise in hamstring injuries (87 vs 114, P=.0847).
records.limitations: Injury data came from public online sources with no exposure data, severity or games missed, and the count comparison cannot separate the absent preseason from COVID-19 disruption, changes to unorganized training, or reporting differences. It covers one season pair, so it shows an association, not a cause.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the study as showing that skipping preseason causes more regular-season injuries, when the design only compares two seasons' counts and cannot isolate the preseason from other 2020 pandemic effects.

records.sourceFile: Relationship Between the Pain Intensity at the Time of the Hamstring Muscle Injury and the Hyperintense T2 Weighted Volume of the Hamstring Muscle Lesion Measured by MRI.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: A retrospective analysis of 61 athletes (recreational, semiprofessional and professional; mainly soccer and track and field) from a prospective multicenter cohort, who had a thigh MRI for suspected acute hamstring injury (mean 7.8 days after injury). The authors report a significant but weak Pearson correlation between pain at injury (NPRS 0 to 10) and the hyperintense T2 volume of the lesion (r=0.287, P=0.025), explaining about 8% of the variance, with no differences in pain by Peetrons grade (P=0.408) or by muscle head (P=0.394).
records.limitations: The sample is small (61), pain was recalled retrospectively in a questionnaire, and only one clinical variable was tested. Table 1 also gives percentages inconsistent with the counts (for example 6 patients with no injury shown as 14.6%, which is 6 of 41, not 61), and the text states 81% single lesions while the table gives 72.1%.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the significant correlation as a usable way to estimate hamstring lesion size from how much pain the athlete felt, when pain at injury explains only about 8% of the variance and the authors conclude it is not enough to indicate lesion extent.

records.sourceFile: Relationship between Neck Musculature and Head Kinematics during a Collision in University American Football Players.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Observational study of 22 players from one university American football team. Isometric neck strength in four directions (handheld dynamometer) and neck circumference were measured before the season, and head linear and angular acceleration were recorded in collisions over seven competition games with an impact-sensing mouthguard. Spearman correlations found a weak negative association between the top 10% of linear acceleration and neck flexor strength (r = -0.344) and very weak to weak negative associations between head kinematics and neck circumference (r = -0.133 to -0.354); lateral flexor strength showed a very weak positive association with angular acceleration (r = 0.121).
records.limitations: Twenty-two players from one team give a small sample, the significant correlations were mostly very weak or weak, and they are unadjusted for confounders such as body size or position. The authors note that correlations cannot show cause and that the timing of neck muscle activation, not measured here, may matter more than peak strength.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read a stronger neck as proof that neck training prevents concussion; the study found weak associations with head kinematics in one small team and did not measure concussion incidence or a training effect.

records.sourceFile: Relationship between athletes' history of stressors and sport injury - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of 19 studies (4156 athletes; 18 prospective, 1 cross-sectional), searched in seven databases from January 2000 to September 2023. The pooled association between athletes' history of stressors (life events, daily hassles, previous injury) and sport injury was small but significant (r = .12, 95% CI .08 to .16). In the results, the association was stronger in adults than adolescents, in contact than non-contact sports, in non-elite than elite athletes, and with general rather than sport-specific stress measures.
records.limitations: The pooled effect is small and heterogeneity was high (I2 = 83.13), so the estimate summarises a wide range of study results. Moderator subgroups rest on few studies, publication bias tests disagreed, and several abstract statistics do not match the results section.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could treat stress history as a strong predictor of injury for individual athletes; the pooled association is small and reflects group-level correlations across heterogeneous studies.

records.sourceFile: Relationship between cognitive performance and lower extremity biomechanics - Implications for sports-related concussion.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Controlled laboratory study of 20 NCAA Division I athletes with prior sports-related concussion (9 men, 11 women; mean 461 days since last concussion, all clinically cleared) and 20 controls matched by sport, position, sex and age. Participants performed unanticipated land-and-cut tasks while lower extremity biomechanics and a functional visuomotor reaction time were recorded, and completed ImPACT and Senaptec cognitive tests. In the concussion group, slower functional reaction time was moderately correlated with reduced knee flexion, and larger dominant-limb knee abduction moment was moderately correlated with lower ImPACT Visual Memory (r = -0.539) and with ImPACT Reaction Time (r = 0.515).
records.limitations: Twenty athletes per group, a single cross-sectional session and many correlations tested without correction mean several significant findings could be chance. Correlations were run separately within each group and many did not differ between groups, and no injury outcomes were measured, so the study cannot show that cognitive deficits cause riskier mechanics or injury.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read this as showing that poor cognitive scores after concussion predict knee injury; the study measured correlations with laboratory mechanics in 40 athletes and recorded no injuries.

verification.residualConcerns: Health-status tag is a judgment call: the exposure group had prior concussions but were cleared and symptom status is not reported. Abstract and results disagree on the direction label for ImPACT Reaction Time.

records.sourceFile: Relationship between trunk and pelvic rotation angles during throwing and the Kerlan–Jobe Orthopedic Clinic score in American football quarterbacks.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Cross-sectional study of 11 healthy quarterbacks (age 18 to 36) from one Japanese university team and one club team, each making five maximum-effort throws at 20 and 30 yards. Trunk rotation, pelvic rotation and hip-shoulder separation, measured with a markerless iPad app (PitchAI), were correlated with the self-reported Kerlan-Jobe Orthopedic Clinic (KJOC) shoulder and elbow score. Several positive correlations were found with individual KJOC items, for example trunk rotation at maximum external rotation (20 yards) with item 3 (rs = 0.709) and pelvic rotation at ball release (30 yards) with item 4 (rs = 0.760).
records.limitations: Eleven players is far below the 84 the authors calculated were needed, and many angle-item correlations were tested without correction, so some significant results may be chance. KJOC scores showed a ceiling effect, and the app's validity for quarterback throwing has not been tested.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read these correlations as evidence that a given throwing mechanic protects the shoulder or elbow; the study correlated app-measured angles with a self-reported score in 11 healthy quarterbacks at one time point.

findings: added further significant correlations with items 5, 7 and 10 reported in results

records.sourceFile: Rescheduling Part 2 of the 11+   reduces injury burden and increases compliance in semi-professional   football.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Cluster randomised controlled trial in which 25 semi-professional (sub-elite) football clubs were randomly allocated to the standard 11+ warm-up, performed in full at the start of training, or to a P2post version, with Parts 1 and 3 at the start and Part 2 moved to the end of training. The 806 male players were followed through the 2017 season, with exposure, 11+ dose and time-loss injuries recorded by on-site trainers. Injury incidence was similar between groups (11.8 vs 12.3 per 1000 h, IRR 1.0). The P2post group completed more 11+ sessions (29.1 vs 18.9), had fewer severe injuries (over 28 days lost) and fewer total days lost to injury (4303 vs 5815), and had a possibly lower ankle injury incidence, but more quadriceps and contusion injuries.
records.limitations: The trial was run in one season in one country and with male semi-professional players only, and the authors caution against applying it to youth or women. Groups differed in 11+ dose as well as timing, so the benefit cannot be attributed to the scheduling change alone, and several subgroup analyses were run on the same data.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the lower injury burden as proof that moving Part 2 to the end of training is the reason injuries fell, when the groups also differed in how often players completed the 11+ and the subgroup findings were exploratory.

changes: paper.methods: 2016 baseline comparison used only a subset of players ('Standard-11+, n = 185 and P2post, n = 226'), not the full cohort

paper.findings / evidenceSummary: ankle, quadriceps and contusion differences are clinical inferences with non-significant p-values (ankle 'Possibly beneficial', p = .132; quadriceps 'Possibly harmful', p = .098; contusion 'Likely harmful', p = .116); added this qualification
paper.limitations: added Results vs Discussion conflict on the P2post reduction from 2016 ('38% and 35%, respectively' vs 'P2post = 40% reduction')
paper.tldr: attribution to compliance stated as the authors' suggestion ('plausible that the benefits ... are related to a dose effect')
paper.athleteDev: replaced generic monitoring advice with the injury-site trade-offs the trial reported
verification.residualConcerns: Players are paid semi-professional (Tier 2 and 3, sub-elite); the 'Professional / Elite' level tag may need reviewer confirmation.

records.sourceFile: Rethinking acute sports injuries - Evidence for an overuse mechanism in hamstring and ACL injuries.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Brief narrative review arguing that hamstring strain and ACL injuries may partly be overuse injuries caused by mechanical fatigue, with no structured search described. It draws on three hamstring case studies that found no kinematic or kinetic deviation in the injury stride compared with preceding strides, on animal and cadaveric repetitive-loading experiments, and on ACL explant analyses. The author reports that repeated simulated landings caused ACL failure at loads below ultimate strength, and states that further research is needed to test the hypothesis.
records.limitations: The evidence is indirect: three hamstring case studies, cadaveric and animal models (mostly middle-aged cadavers and animal calf muscles), one explant comparison, and small imaging studies such as three professional Alpine skiers, with no in vivo measure of the nano- and microscale damage the hypothesis depends on. Because it is a hypothesis-driven narrative review with no described search or appraisal, it cannot establish how common overuse-type hamstring or ACL injuries are.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could treat the proposed overuse mechanism as established and start load-based restrictions for hamstring or ACL risk before the mechanism has been tested in living athletes.

changes: screeningLimitations: 'no in vivo measures of tissue damage' overstated; the review cites in vivo imaging (ACL T2 relaxation 'in three professional Alpine skiers', ACL CSA over a soccer season) -> no in vivo measure of nano- and microscale damage

records.sourceFile: Return to full participation following concussion in the National Football League, 2015 through 2020.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: A retrospective cohort study of 1,480 team-related concussions in 1,121 NFL players across the 2015 to 2020 seasons, using electronic health record and league participation data. The median time missed was 9 days (mean 15.0), with an average of 3,639 player-days and 255 games lost per year, and 59% of players who were concussed in the regular season or preseason missed at least one game. No player returned to competition on the day of injury, and 37.7% of players concussed in a Sunday game played the following Sunday.
records.limitations: This is an observational study with no comparison group, and it does not measure symptom count, severity or neuropsychological test results, which the authors note predict return timing. Days and games were imputed for 8% and 13% of cases, and time lost depends on the timing of injury within the season and on roster decisions.
records.synthesisCaution: The 9-day median could be read as a recovery benchmark for any individual player, when it describes a league-wide protocol-driven timeline for professional football players and cannot predict one player's return.

changes: populations: added Male Athletes, since the NFL sample is described as male ("the concussed player can clear multiple phases in a single day if he remains asymptomatic")
paper.limitations: imputation described as '8% of days and 13% of games' -> 8% and 13% of concussions in the days and games analyses ("days: n = 118; 8%; games: n = 185, 13%")
verification.residualConcerns: Clinically sensitive (concussion return to play). The paper is internally inconsistent: the discussion gives annual burden as 3,591 days versus 3,639 in results, and special teams burden as 485 versus 492 days; methods say missing-return cases were both imputed and excluded from days-missed calculations. Several authors are NFL employees or paid consultants.

records.sourceFile: Return to play after sports hernia surgery.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: A clinical review of sports hernia (inguinal disruption) covering definition, diagnosis, imaging, nonoperative and operative treatment, and rehabilitation after repair. The review cites a randomized trial of 30 operated and 30 physiotherapy athletes, in which 27 of 30 (90%) operated athletes returned to sport at 3 months versus 8 of 30 (27%) nonoperated, and case series reporting return rates of about 80% to 100% after open and laparoscopic repair. The authors describe laparoscopic return in about 2 to 6 weeks and open repair in 1 to 6 months, with a rehabilitation protocol in three phases over about 8 weeks.
records.limitations: No literature search is described, and most surgical outcomes come from uncontrolled surgical case series, often with different techniques and patient groups. The review notes that there is little research on return-to-sport timing and that the rehabilitation phases are the authors' institutional practice, not a tested protocol.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could treat the 80% to 100% return rates and the 2 to 6 week laparoscopic timeline as expected outcomes for their own athletes, when they come mostly from uncontrolled series of selected surgical patients.

changes: screeningLimitations and paper.limitations: 'surgeon-reported results' is not stated in the text -> now uncontrolled surgical case series with differing techniques and populations ("direct comparison of these outcomes is difficult because of different patient populations and a variety of surgical techniques")

records.sourceFile: Return to play guidelines after cervical spine injuries in American football athletes - A literature-based review.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Literature-based review of 28 studies (PubMed and EMBASE, English-language, published by 1 December 2019) on return to play after cervical spine injury in NFL and NCAA football athletes, mostly case series, case studies, expert panels and injury surveillance data. The authors report average return times after nonoperative care, canal-diameter thresholds for stenosis, and post-fusion recommendations, and they propose guiding principles rather than validated rules.
records.limitations: The review pools no data and relies largely on case-based and expert-consensus sources with little clinical detail, so it cannot set a validated clearance standard for any cervical diagnosis. Its search reached only English-language papers up to December 2019.
records.synthesisCaution: The 'guidelines' are the authors' consensus-based principles, so staff could read the canal-diameter thresholds (about 10 mm and under 8 mm) or the average return times as firm clearance rules.

verification.residualConcerns: Cervical spine return-to-play paper; recommendations are largely expert opinion. Citation has no volume or pages because the text is the publish-ahead-of-print version.

records.sourceFile: Return to play in professional football players following traumatic cervical spine injury - Expert opinions from the National Football League spine surgeons.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Cross-sectional online survey of 26 NFL team spine consultants (from 49 invited, covering 21 of 32 teams) answering five hypothetical cervical injury vignettes on management and return-to-play criteria. Most favoured anterior cervical discectomy and fusion for symptomatic disc herniation (73% for radiculopathy, 88% for myelopathy), a rigid orthosis for nondisplaced unilateral facet fracture (68%) and single-level fusion for facet dislocation (56%). Six months was the most common time to full professional play for both disc vignettes (42% and 38%).
records.limitations: The sample is 26 consultants' opinions on hypothetical vignettes, not outcomes in players, so the study cannot show which treatment or clearance timing returns players to play more safely. The authors state the results are not a consensus statement or return-to-play guideline.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the common 6-month return timeline or the fusion-based clearance criteria as a validated standard, when they reflect how a small group of consultants answered hypothetical cases.

records.sourceFile: Return to play, performance, and economic analysis of National Football League players after Lisfrance injury.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Case series of 33 NFL players with Lisfranc injuries from the 2009 to 2020 seasons, identified from public records and verified by at least two sources. Of these, 27 (81.8%) returned to play at a median of 11.0 months, and snap counts and games played did not change significantly. Approximate value fell significantly in the first season back (median 6.0 to 5.0, P = .022), and the authors estimate $104.7 million (2022 US dollars) in salary cost for games missed by returning players.
records.limitations: Players were found through public reports, so unreported cases are missing, and the approximate value metric is unvalidated. Per-position groups are 2 to 8 players, so the study is underpowered and cannot separate injury type, treatment or rehabilitation effects.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the 81.8% return rate as a reassuring expectation for any player, or the $104.7 million figure as a true financial cost, when the sample is small, public-record based and the cost is a salary estimate for missed games.

changes: paper.findings: '23 of 26 operated players were still active two seasons later' -> 23 of 26 players injured through 2019 remained in the NFL 2 seasons after injury ('88.5% (23 of 26) remaining in the NFL for 2 seasons ... adjusted to include only players injured through 2019')
paper.findings: added that non-returners were older and had longer NFL tenure (31.0 vs 26.0 y, P = .007; 8.5 vs 3.0 y, P = .008)
paper.athleteDev: clarified the 23% AV and 9% snap declines are untested means across 22 players (Table 4)
populations: added 'Male Athletes' (NFL players; text refers to 'his in-season availability')

records.sourceFile: Return to sports following distal biceps tendon repair - A current concepts review.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Narrative review of return to sport after distal biceps tendon repair in athletes, drawing on four studies: 10 weightlifters (D'Alessandro), 61 analysed athletes from mixed sports (Gowd), 35 NFL players (McGinnis) and 22 NFL players (Pagani). The authors report a pooled return to sport of 95.3%, a return to the same level of 81.8%, and a mean time to return of 38.8 weeks. No search method, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal is described.
records.limitations: The review draws on four small, mostly retrospective series with different sports, outcomes and rehabilitation protocols, and it reports no confounder adjustment. The pooled return rate cannot be reproduced from the per-study counts, so the evidence cannot set clearance criteria or an individual return timeline.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the 95% return rate as a likely outcome for any athlete, when it comes from small series, mostly of NFL players and weightlifters, with no comparison group and a possible loss of athletes with complications.

paper.tldr: muddled 'usually to the same level only after about 39 weeks' -> separated return rate, same-level rate and mean time
paper.findings: Pagani '84% (21 of 22)' presented as consistent -> noted that 21 of 22 does not equal the reported 84%
paper.limitations: added the Pagani and dominant-side odds ratio conflicts (text OR 6.370 vs Table 2 OR 0.749)
paper.athleteDev: unsupported reasoning about strength deficits -> rehabilitation protocols reported in only two studies and 'not evidence based'
